xperienced people into employment through a dedicated employability pathway and free online skills resources. Designed with input from people who have lived experience of care, the programme is available across all John Lewis Partnership locations.

The programme includes a welcome tour, job shadowing, interview skills training and an interview. Successful candidates are offered suitable vacancies where available. Those who pass the interview but cannot be placed immediately may join a talent pool for up to 3 months and be contacted when opportunities arise.

Care-experienced people who work for the organisation can join a dedicated colleague network led by people with lived experience, and dedicated wellbeing support is also available. Managers and workplace buddies involved in the programme complete Care Aware training, helping them understand the barriers care-experienced people may face and how to create a more supportive working environment. The organisation offers a wide range of opportunities to boost skills and help people progress, including apprenticeships.

A free online employability platform offers practical support, including CV writing and interview preparation.

Digital skills and online safety

The ability to navigate online spaces safely and confidently is essential for accessing education, employment, financial services, health information and social support. There is significant benefit from practical, non-judgmental training for care-experienced young people, particularly for those who have not benefited from peer or parental oversight on online safety previously.

Local authorities should consider, alongside what financial support can be offered for access to broadband, what support can be provided to care-experienced young people as part of their local offer, including in areas such as:

how to spot scams, phishing and deepfakes

understanding online grooming and exploitation behaviours

managing social media privacy settings

recognising online hate or radicalisation

safe use of dating apps and sharing images

protecting personal data, especially when applying for jobs or housing

Developing and publishing the local offer

This section contains details on:

developing the local offer with care-experienced people

recognising different identities and experiences

additional considerations when developing the local offer

publishing and updating the local offer

format of the local offer

Developing the local offer with care-experienced people

When developing their local offer, local authorities are required to consult with relevant persons, which means care-experienced young people, and organisations or people that represent and support care-experienced young people.

Local authorities should consider how best to engage and consult with as many of their care-experienced young people as possible. We expect local authorities to work with their care-experienced young people to co-produce a local offer that is meaningful and reflects the needs, views and wishes of the care-experienced young people they are responsible for.

Recognising different identities and experiences

Care leavers will differ in:

ethnicity

culture

religion

gender identity

sexual orientation

disability or neurodiversity

Recognising diversity ensures that services are inclusive and culturally competent.

Local authorities have obligations under the Equality Act 2010 to prevent discrimination and actively promote inclusion and fairness.

Local authorities should ensure that the local offer is shaped by input from care leavers from underrepresented groups, which will:

help the offer reflect real needs

ensure the offer is relevant and practical

empower young people to have a voice

Additional considerations when developing the local offer

Local authorities will want to consider what additional non-statutory support is required to meet the needs of their cohort of care-experienced young people.

The local offer must include, and should differentiate between, both care-experienced young people’s statutory entitlements and other additional support that local authorities choose to provide.

The local offer should:

reflect support offered by all local authority departments, not only children’s services, including housing, education, leisure services, public health, youth services, libraries, employment and skills, transport, welfare and financial support teams and community safety

include, as part of the offer, any discrete service provided by a partner organisation for care-experienced young people, such as a health drop-in exclusively for care-experienced young people, where the local authority is confident that there is an ongoing commitment from that organisation to provide that service or support

signpost or provide links to services provided by partner organisations that are available to all young people, such as a young people’s sexual health clinic or a careers advice service for 16 to 25 year-olds, where this is more appropriate. The local offer should also explain what support the local authority can provide to help care-experienced young people access those services – for example, help with making referrals, arranging appointments, accompanying them where appropriate or covering travel costs if needed

Publishing and updating the local offer

Once local authorities have consulted on and published their local offer, it must be updated from time to time and should be reviewed regularly to ensure that the services on offer reflect what care-experienced young people need most.

Local authorities can choose how regularly they review their local offer, but we would expect local authorities to update it at least every 2 years, following further consultation with care-experienced young people.

Local authorities should clearly explain how former UASC care-experienced young people can access the local offer and the support outlined in this guidance – further information is included in benefits and entitlements.

The local offer should include information on:

access to legal advice on asylum or immigration matters

advocacy and independent advice

how to request an assessment of needs if “No Recourse to Public Funds” conditions limit access to parts of the local offer

support to reduce isolation and build social networks, including mentoring, befriending and community programmes

holistic support that considers language needs, cultural identity, mental health vulnerabilities and specialist services to help young people settle safely and move towards independence

Local authorities should ensure that:

where a young person is eligible to apply for permission to work, they are made aware of this opportunity and supported to access appropriate advice and assistance to make an application where appropriate

where a young person is eligible to access education, they are made aware of this and are supported to understand what opportunities are available to them and how they can be accessed

Education, training and employment

This section includes details on:

education and training, including:

further education

the 16 to 19 bursary fund

apprenticeships

higher education

employment, including a case study

digital skills and online safety

Education and training

Care-experienced young people should have access to comprehensive support to help them achieve their education, training and employment goals. They should be encouraged to pursue ambitious opportunities that match their interests, abilities and potential.

The local offer should:

explain the support available to help care leavers access and sustain education, employment and training, including employability support, work experience, mentoring, internships and support to re-engage with suitable opportunities where they are not currently participating

provide clear access to personalised careers information, advice and guidance, covering education, training and employment opportunities – information should help care leavers understand how different courses and qualifications can support progression into further learning, apprenticeships, HE and employment

outline local financial assistance for care leavers, such as travel costs, equipment grants, interview clothing, rent and council tax support, apprenticeship start-up funding and accommodation outside university term time

You should present this information in clear, accessible sections to help care leavers quickly identify the support most relevant to their chosen pathway.

The local offer should also include details about:

the statutory entitlements as set out in the Children Act 1989 to support care-experienced young people with financial assistance if they require it (sections 23C(4)(a) and 24B(1) of the 1989 Act)

financial support available to young people participating in FE, HE and apprenticeships

accommodation support for young people participating in FE or HE

links or details of universal sources of information, including careers guidance and financial support

Further education

The section on FE within the local offer should summarise information on the types of courses available for learners aged 16 to 19 and over 19 to encourage care leavers to be aware of the different pathways available to them. It should include information on technical and vocational qualifications, including how to access advice and guidance about them.

For care leavers aged over 19, the offer should note the range of level 2 and 3 free courses. This includes free courses to achieve GCSE English and maths, and the Free courses for jobs offer, which includes a range of fully funded courses at level 3.

It should set out the main types of financial support available in FE, including the 16 to 19 bursary fund, childcare support and learner support for learners aged over 19, which operates in a similar way to the 16 to 19 bursary fund. National Careers Service includes further information on courses and financial support.

16 to 19 bursary fund

The 16 to 19 bursary fund is delivered through 2 streams:

the defined vulnerable group bursary

the discretionary bursary

Care-experienced young people and care leavers with financial need may be eligible for the defined vulnerable group bursary, which provides enhanced support of up to £1,200 per year.

The local offer should set out advice for how students can apply, via their education provider, who will assess their eligibility and funding needs. The bursary can help cover essential costs such as travel, meals and course equipment.

The discretionary bursary is allocated directly to schools and colleges, which set their own eligibility criteria and determine the level of support based on individual need. There is no fixed limit on the amount institutions can award, and they may use additional funding from their own budgets where affordable. Providers can also use the discretionary bursary to top up the defined vulnerable group bursary if further support is needed.

Most schools and colleges provide information about the 16 to 19 bursary fund on their websites so links to these may be useful in the local offer. Students can also contact student support services for advice and guidance.

Case study: regional approach to the local offer

The Greater Manchester Care Leaver Guarantee is all about providing support and opportunities to our young people that have been in care.

All 10 Greater Manchester local authorities, along with a wide range of partners, have joined together to create a series of entitlements and offers that will help care leavers live happy and healthy lives. All 10 local authorities have agreed that, as a guarantee, care leavers are entitled to the following (the list is not exhaustive but illustrates what can be done in the regions):

local free prescriptions

housing providers will work with care leavers to give them the knowledge and support they need so the move into their own home is a success, as well as practical help including managing a tenancy, paying bills and budgeting

exemption from paying council tax up to age 25 across all local authorities

a £3,000 leaving care grant when they move into their property

a clear set of financial entitlements

free travel

Personal adviser support post-21

Local authorities must maintain contact with eligible care-experienced young people until they reach the age of 21, including those in custody.

The local authority’s duty to keep in touch extends beyond their 21st birthday until they reach age 25, while they remain in or begin or resume a programme of education or training for care leavers who are:

former relevant children

persons qualifying for advice and assistance aged up to 25 who are pursuing a programme of education or training

Eligible care-experienced young people can request personal adviser (PA) support at any time up to reaching age 25. If PA support is requested, the local authority must:

allocate a PA

review or refresh the pathway plan

provide support tailored to their assessed needs

If an eligible care leaver is not receiving advice and support (including a PA and pathway plan), the local authority must offer it as soon as possible after the young person reaches age 21 and at least once every 12 months.

It is important to include in the local offer how eligible care-experienced young people can access or re-engage with this continued support if they require it and have lost contact with the local authority. This should include an email or web contact, or a helpline if available.

Staying Close support

Staying Close helps care leavers make a successful transition to adulthood by strengthening the relationships, networks and practical support around them. The focus of this support is setting them up to find and keep a home that is right for them. Staying Close will become a national duty in 2028 to 2029 and will be rolled out to local authorities nationally in advance of this.

Where Staying Close is available in the local area, local authorities should include it within their local offer as part of the support available to young people leaving care and set out clearly how young people can access it.

Domestic abuse

Many care-experienced young people entered care as a result of domestic abuse, neglect or other forms of family harm, and some may return to the same families, communities or local areas in which that harm occurred.

Local authorities must comply with their duties under the Domestic Abuse Act 2021, and in developing their local offer, should have regard to provisions of the Act, including its wider statutory definition of domestic abuse and the recognition that children are victims of domestic abuse in their own right where they see, hear or experience its effects.

The local offer should clearly set out:

what support is available to care-experienced young people who are experiencing, or are at risk of, domestic abuse

information on access to specialist domestic abuse services, advocacy, safe accommodation and support to relocate where appropriate

Services and support

This section includes details on the services and support local authorities should include in the local offer.

This includes:

relationships

participation in society

voting and the democratic process

additional needs

care leavers living or placed outside of their local authority, including a case study

transitions to adult services and mental health support

health and wellbeing

custody

young parents

former UASC and migrant children leaving care

Relationships

Strong, stable and supportive relationships are essential for care-experienced young people as they move towards adult life. When care-experienced young people have at least one such relationship in their lives, they experience better educational, physical and mental health outcomes, are less likely to engage in risky behaviours and demonstrate increased resilience.

Local authorities should consider:

how young people can maintain enduring relationships that continue to offer emotional security, consistent responsiveness and dependability

the services and support available to help care-experienced young people develop and maintain positive social networks, and to understand what healthy, safe and nurturing relationships look like

Where this support is available, the local offer should include detail about what is offered and how young people can access it, including:

relational interactions with PAs, whose interest should be in the overall wellbeing and development of the young person – the PA should be empowered to interact with and make decisions alongside the young person in a way that makes them feel that they belong and are cared for and supported

support to reconnect safely with former carers, relatives or other important adults, where this is appropriate and in the young person’s best interests
